Stunting in Peruvian children aged 6-59 months

Dataset 5: Peru DHS child anaemia and growth extract

RSR feasibility analysis

2026-08-03

Introduction

Stunting – height-for-age more than two standard deviations below the WHO reference median – is the standard indicator of chronic childhood undernutrition and a strong predictor of later cognitive and economic outcomes. Peru has halved its national stunting prevalence since 2005, but the remaining burden is heavily concentrated in highland and jungle communities and in the poorest households. The Peruvian Demographic and Health Survey (ENDES) measures every surveyed child aged 6-59 months and links the measurement to birth history, maternal characteristics, household wealth and geography.

Aim. Among Peruvian children aged 6-59 months, we examined which of child age, child sex, birth-weight category, maternal education, household wealth, natural region and maternal indigenous identity are independently associated with stunting, mutually adjusting for the others.

This is a Purpose 3 analysis: several predictors are of interest and the question is which remain associated with the outcome after mutual adjustment.

Methods

Data source. A cross-sectional extract of 19191 children aged 6-59 months from the Peru Demographic and Health Survey (ENDES), a nationally implemented household survey, each linked to their mother’s interview and household record.

Variables. The outcome is stunting, defined as height-for-age Z-score below -2; the modelled event is stunting = Yes. Predictors are child age in months (continuous, 6-59); child sex (reference Female); maternally reported birth-weight category (reference Normal, versus Low i.e. below 2.5 kg and Macrosomia); mother’s highest education (reference Primary or none); household wealth quintile (reference Poorest); natural region (reference Lima metropolitan); and maternal indigenous identity (reference No).

height_for_age_z is excluded by construction: stunting is exactly height_for_age_z < -2, so including the Z-score would give a perfectly separating, meaningless model. Haemoglobin and anaemia are also excluded because they are co-outcomes of undernutrition rather than exposures. survey_weight is never a predictor.

Statistical analysis. Logistic regression via glm(family = binomial), justified because the outcome is binary; estimates are reported as odds ratios. We fitted a univariable model for each predictor first, then a single multivariable model containing all of them. Predictors were chosen in advance on subject-matter grounds, not by significance. Significance threshold 0.05; estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals. Assumptions were checked with performance::check_model(). Analysis used R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) with tidyverse, gtsummary and performance.

Missing data. Complete-case analysis: 18640 of 19191 rows were analysed (551 dropped, 2.9%). Essentially all the loss is missing maternally reported birth weight.

12.2% of children (2280 of 18640) were stunted. The socio-economic concentration is extreme: 24.7% of children in the poorest quintile versus 2.6% in the richest, an approximately 9.5-fold difference in prevalence. Stunted children are also over-represented in the highlands and jungle, in indigenous households and among those reported as low birth weight.

Exploratory figure

Figure 1. Prevalence of stunting by household wealth quintile and reported birth-weight category.

Both gradients run in the same direction: within every wealth quintile low-birth-weight children are stunted two to three times as often as normal-birth-weight children (and macrosomic children least often of all), and within every birth-weight category prevalence falls steeply as wealth rises – from roughly half of low-birth-weight children in the poorest quintile to under a tenth in the richest.

Low birth weight is the strongest child-level predictor: reported birth weight under 2.5 kg carries 3.26 times the crude odds of stunting (95% CI 2.85 to 3.72, p < 0.001), while macrosomia is strongly protective (OR 0.36). The social contrasts are larger still: highland residence carries 6.6 times the odds of Lima, maternal indigenous identity 3.7 times, and the richest quintile has 92% lower odds than the poorest. Every predictor including child sex is significant crudely, which at this sample size says little on its own.

Why adjustment is needed

The crude odds ratios overlap heavily and cannot be read side by side. Household wealth confounds the regional and ethnic contrasts: the highlands and jungle contain most of the poorest quintile while Lima contains almost none of it, and poverty independently determines diet, sanitation and health-service access, so a crude highlands OR of 6.6 is substantially a poverty estimate. Maternal education does the same for wealth and ethnicity: better-educated mothers live in richer households, are less often indigenous, and independently practise better infant feeding, so schooling and wealth each absorb part of the other’s crude effect. Birth weight is itself socially patterned, so the crude birth-weight OR partly reflects the maternal circumstances that produced the small baby. And child age matters because stunting prevalence peaks in the second year of life and the age composition is not identical across quintiles or regions. Mutual adjustment is required before any single association can be described as independent.

The model has AIC 1.19725^{4} with 15 parameters and 2280 events, giving 162.9 events per parameter – well above the conventional minimum of 10, so the model is stably estimated. Conditional on the other six predictors, low birth weight retains 3.18 times the odds of stunting (95% CI 2.75 to 3.68) and macrosomia 0.45 times (95% CI 0.35 to 0.58), so birth-weight category alone spans a roughly 7-fold range in adjusted odds. The wealth gradient remains monotonic, with the richest quintile at 0.21 times the odds of the poorest (95% CI 0.15 to 0.3), and highland residence at 2.63 times Lima. Each additional month of age is associated with 1.4% lower adjusted odds, and boys have 1.13 times the odds of girls (p = 0.011).

The social variables move most, all toward the null. Maternal indigenous identity collapses from OR 3.73 crude to 1.44 adjusted: most of the raw excess was wealth, education and region, though a real independent association survives. Highland residence falls from 6.56 to 2.63 and higher maternal education rises from 0.17 to 0.41, both large moves toward 1. The richest-versus-poorest contrast also attenuates markedly, from 0.08 to 0.21, because the wealth quintiles differ systematically in maternal schooling and region. In contrast, low birth weight barely moves (3.26 to 3.18) and child age barely moves (0.987 to 0.986): both are essentially uncorrelated with the household covariates, so no adjustment was needed for them. Macrosomia is the one estimate that moves appreciably in a partly explanatory direction, from 0.36 to 0.45; large babies are commoner in better-off households, so part of its crude protective effect was socio-economic. No predictor changes significance status. Given 18640 observations that is unsurprising, and the useful comparison is between the sizes of the attenuations, not between p-values.

Diagnostics

For a logistic model the relevant panels are as follows. Binned residuals: only 31.4% of bins fall inside the error bounds against a rule-of-thumb target of about 95%, which is a clear signal of mis-specification. The cause is visible in the data: stunting prevalence rises from about 12% at 6-11 months to about 18% at 12-23 months and then falls back to about 9% by four years, so a single linear log-odds slope in age cannot follow it, and the model systematically under-predicts risk in the second year of life. A spline or an age-group factor would fix this. Collinearity is low throughout (maximum VIF 1.64), so the wealth, education, region and ethnicity coefficients are separately estimable despite their strong pairwise associations. Influential observations show no points beyond the Cook’s distance contours. Events per parameter is 162.9, so sparse-data bias and overfitting are not concerns, although some individual cells are thin – there are only 67 stunted macrosomic children in the whole file, and only a handful of stunted children in the Lima / richest cell, so any interaction involving those groups would be unstable. Homogeneity of variance and normality of residuals are printed by check_model() for completeness but do not apply to a binomial GLM.

Discussion

Stunting in Peruvian preschool children is driven jointly by birth endowment and household circumstances. A child reported as low birth weight has about 3.2 times the odds of stunting compared with a normal-birth-weight child of the same sex, age, region, ethnicity, maternal schooling and household wealth – and that estimate is essentially unchanged by adjustment, so it is not merely a marker of poverty. On top of that, moving from the poorest to the richest quintile is associated with roughly 79% lower adjusted odds, and highland residence with about 2.6 times the odds of Lima. Practically this supports a two-pronged approach: antenatal care that reduces low birth weight, and continued postnatal nutrition programming targeted at poor highland and jungle households.

Limitations. Cross-sectional design; all estimates are associations, not causal effects. The outcome is a dichotomised continuous measurement – the same information analysed on the continuous HAZ scale has more power and does not depend on an arbitrary cut-point, so the continuous analysis should be preferred where possible. Birth weight is a maternally reported three-level category, not a measured weight in kilograms, and is therefore subject to recall bias that is likely worse among less-educated mothers, exactly the group with the highest stunting risk; this would bias the birth-weight OR toward the null. The source ENDES analysis used the DHS complex design – cluster (HV001), stratum (HV022) and sampling weights – whereas this extract carries only the weight variable, which is deliberately not used here; standard errors are therefore too narrow, estimates are not design-corrected, and this sample must not be described as nationally representative. With 18640 rows almost every comparison is statistically significant, so interpretation must lead with effect sizes rather than p-values. The single strongest known determinant of child height, maternal height, is not in this extract at all, and neither are birth order, birth interval, infection history or dietary diversity, so residual confounding is certain. The binned-residual check fails, so the age term is mis-specified. Finally, the 551 rows dropped for missing birth weight are unlikely to be missing completely at random.

Future work. Refit with the DHS survey design, an age spline, and maternal height and birth order from the fuller ENDES recode file.

Feasibility notes

Not part of a student report.

  • Works statistically. 2280 events, 162.9 events per parameter, no separation, maximum VIF 1.64, large and interpretable odds ratios. This is a safe logistic exercise.
  • FATAL trap: the deterministic twin. stunting is exactly height_for_age_z < -2. Including the Z-score gives perfect separation. This must be flagged in the brief; it is the most likely way a student wrecks this analysis.
  • Redundant with the HAZ outcome. This is the same question as height_for_age_z, run on a coarsened version of the same measurement. Students should do one or the other; the continuous version is statistically better and the binary version is the better logistic-regression exercise.
  • Binned residuals fail badly (31.4% within bounds). Worse than the anaemia model, because the age-stunting relationship is non-monotonic (peak around 18 months). Usable as a teaching point, but a student will need guidance or will simply report that diagnostics were fine.
  • Some thin cells. Only 67 stunted macrosomic children, and only single-digit stunted counts in the Lima / richest-quintile cell. The main effects model is fine; any interaction with those groups is not.
  • Birth weight is categorical, not kg. The codebook wording invites students to treat birth_weight as continuous. It is a three-level string, and the two non-reference levels point in opposite directions.
  • Sample size. At 18640 rows everything is significant; the brief must force effect-size-led interpretation.
  • Design not honoured. Only the weight is present, not cluster or stratum, so a design-correct analysis is impossible from this extract.
